ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Thickness Inspection in Grand Rapids, Michigan
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes ultrasonic testing technicians to Grand Rapids and West Michigan sites for wall-thickness surveys on tanks, vessels, boiler and process piping, plus shear-wave examination of structural and pressure welds. Send us the drawings, the governing code and a description of the access you have, and we will build the scope around it. Request a UT quote for your Grand Rapids job and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Grand Rapids

Grand Rapids is a manufacturing metro first and a refinery or port town not at all, and that shapes what ultrasonic testing is asked to do here. The Right Place, the regional economic development group, counts more than 127,000 advanced manufacturing jobs across West Michigan, and the region is known for office furniture, automotive supply, plastics, food processing and production tooling. Each of those industries runs equipment that wears from the inside.

  • Food and beverage plants: steam headers, hot-water and glycol piping, jacketed kettles, brewing and fermentation tanks, and compressed-air receivers. Stainless vessels thin by pitting and crevice attack that a visual check cannot see.
  • Plastics and extrusion plants: steam and thermal-oil piping, hydraulic accumulators and chiller shells, many of them installed decades ago and rarely opened.
  • Furniture, tooling and metal fabrication shops: structural frames for presses and conveyors, crane runway beams, pressure vessels for paint and powder-coating lines, and welded tube assemblies.
  • Utilities and campus plants: boilers and heat exchangers at hospitals, universities and district heating loops, and natural gas distribution piping and station equipment as utilities replace aging mains.
  • Bridges and highway steel: the Grand River crossings and the interchange structures around US-131 and I-196 carry steel girders and bearings whose welded details are examined under bridge rules.

The common thread is that most of this equipment is not on a refinery inspection cycle with a full-time inspection department. It sits in plants where a maintenance manager, a plant engineer or an insurer decides when thickness gets measured. We write the scope so that it answers the question that person actually has.

What ultrasonic testing finds, and what it does not

A pulse-echo ultrasonic probe sends a short sound pulse into the material and times the echo from the far surface or from a reflector inside the wall. Thickness gauging turns that time into remaining wall. Weld examination reads the echo from planar flaws such as lack of fusion, cracks and incomplete penetration, and from volumetric flaws such as slag. Ultrasonic testing works on carbon steel, stainless steel, aluminum and many plastics, which suits the mixed materials found in a Grand Rapids plant.

It also has limits that belong in the scope document. Rough, scaled or pitted surfaces scatter sound and can hide the true back wall. Coarse-grained cast stainless attenuates the beam. Thin sections under a few millimeters may need a different probe or a different method. Corrosion that is concentrated in a small pit can be missed between grid points, so the grid spacing is an engineering decision, not a default. Linear indications that run parallel to the sound beam can be invisible to a single angle, which is why weld scans use more than one probe angle and scanning pattern. Where a question is really about surface cracking on a ferromagnetic part, the magnetic particle page for Grand Rapids is the better route.

Thickness surveys on tanks, vessels and piping

Most thickness work starts with a list of condition monitoring locations, usually shortened to CMLs. On a piping circuit those are elbows, tees, reducers, injection points and dead legs. On a vessel they are the shell courses, heads and nozzles. Our technicians mark each location, record a grid when the owner wants one, and gauge it with a dual-element probe, which handles pitted and corroded metal far better than a single-element probe.

Calibration happens on a step block of the same material before the survey and again when the probe, the temperature or the surface changes. On a hot steam line the velocity of sound in steel drops as temperature rises, so the reading is corrected, and a high-temperature probe and couplant are used rather than ordinary gel. On thin or pitted wall the gauge display is kept in A-scan view so the technician can see whether the echo is the back wall or a doubled echo. ASME Section V Article 23 carries the SE-797 practice for contact pulse-echo thickness measurement, and our guide to the thickness measurement requirements walks through the same ground in plainer terms.

Results go into a thickness table or a grid map. The owner's inspector or engineer applies the corrosion-rate and remaining-life calculation. We supply measured data that is traceable to a calibration and a procedure.

Ultrasonic examination of welds

Shear-wave examination uses an angle-beam probe, typically 45, 60 or 70 degrees, on a wedge. The technician builds a reference level or a distance-amplitude curve from side-drilled holes in a reference block, scans from both sides of the weld where access permits, and evaluates indications against the acceptance rules of the construction code. This is the method chosen when a groove weld must be examined through its full volume and a surface method cannot reach the root.

In practice, Grand Rapids work falls into three families. Structural steel under AWS D1.1 has its own ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds, and bridge steel under AWS D1.5 has stricter rules for tension members. Pressure equipment under ASME Section VIII, Division 1 can call for ultrasonic examination under Mandatory Appendix 12. Process piping under ASME B31.3 can call for ultrasonic examination of welds as an alternative or an addition to other examination, with acceptance against Table 341.3.2. A procedure must name which of these governs before a probe touches steel.

Codes, the state and who owns the decision

Michigan regulates boilers and certain pressure vessels through the Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs, Bureau of Construction Codes, Boiler Division, and its rules adopt the National Board Inspection Code by reference for inspection, repair and alteration. The state's chief inspector and deputy inspectors inspect boilers and pressure vessels within the state's scope, and the state has said its inspectors do not perform power piping inspections under ASME B31.1, which leaves piping inspection with the owner. That detail matters for scoping: when a plant asks who decides that a B31.1 line is fit for service, the answer is the owner and whoever the owner designates.

For equipment inspected under API 510, 570 or 653, the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic examination and delivers the data that inspector needs, such as thickness at CMLs or weld indications, and does not take the place of that inspector. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j), the mechanical integrity element of process safety management, applies where a covered process is present. It asks for inspection and testing that follows recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice, and ultrasonic thickness data is one of the usual records offered to show it.

Who performs the work and how it is controlled

Technicians are mobilized to your site and travel to Grand Rapids for the agreed scope. Atlantis has no office in the city. The technicians are qualified under our written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician sets up the equipment, calibrates, performs the examination and interprets the results. An ASNT Level III approves the written procedure and reviews the reports. The company is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001, which governs how records and calibrations are kept, and it describes its method in a written ultrasonic testing offer that owners can compare with their own specification.

If your own written practice or your client's contract names a different edition of the code, or an additional qualification requirement, tell us at the quote stage so the procedure can be written to it. Our Level III consulting can also review a procedure that an owner already holds.

What the report contains

A thickness report identifies each component and location, the procedure and revision, the instrument and probe, the calibration block and the temperature of the surface, the technician and qualification level, the measured value at every point, and the owner's nominal and minimum values for comparison. Weld reports add the scan plan, the probe angles, the reference level, each indication's location along the weld, its length and amplitude, and a plain accept or reject against the named criteria. Sketches and thickness grids are attached where they help the owner's engineer find the spot again years later.

Planning a UT job in Grand Rapids

Winter in West Michigan changes how ultrasonic work is planned. Lake-effect snow, wind off Lake Michigan and long spells below freezing affect outdoor tanks, rooftop equipment and bridge steel. Ordinary couplant stiffens in the cold and a probe loses contact on a frosted surface, so cold-weather work uses low-temperature couplant, surface preparation and often an enclosure or heater. Summer humidity and heat bring the opposite problem on hot lines, where the technician uses high-temperature probes and keeps the contact time short.

Outages at food, plastics and furniture plants often follow shutdown weeks tied to production cycles rather than a refinery turnaround calendar, so the schedule is usually set by the plant. Plan for badging and safety orientation, lock-out and confined-space entry where tank interiors are involved, and scaffolding or lift access where wall measurements sit overhead. Travel is by road and air through Gerald R. Ford International Airport, and we plan the mobilization around your access rules instead of promising an arrival date in advance. Surface preparation is the single biggest driver of data quality: if paint, scale or insulation is in the way, say so when you request the quote.

UT, MT or PT: choosing the method for a Grand Rapids job

Use ultrasonic testing when you need remaining wall, internal corrosion or the volume of a weld. Use magnetic particle inspection when you need surface and near-surface cracks in ferromagnetic steel, such as press frames, crane hooks or weld toes. Use liquid penetrant testing for surface-breaking flaws in stainless steel, aluminum or any non-magnetic material. Many jobs use two of the three on the same component, for example UT for the weld volume and MT for the finished surface. For comparison guidance see the ultrasonic testing guide, or the Michigan service hub at inspection services in Michigan.

Training your own technicians in Grand Rapids

Many plants prefer to keep routine thickness readings in-house and call us for weld examination or the first baseline survey. If that is your plan, our UT Level 1 and UT Level 2 courses cover theory and practice, and the ultrasonic simulator lets a trainee practice calibration and scanning before touching a part. Qualification stays with your company under its written practice, and the SNT-TC-1A eligibility checker shows the hours a candidate needs. See also our NDT training for Grand Rapids page.

faq.q: Can you gauge wall thickness on a tank or vessel that stays in service in Grand Rapids?
faq.a: Yes, in most cases. Contact ultrasonic thickness gauging works on an operating tank or pipe from the outside, provided the surface can be cleaned and the temperature is within the probe's range. We agree access, safe work conditions and the grid with your plant before the technicians are mobilized.

faq.q: How do you handle pitted or corroded surfaces when measuring thickness?
faq.a: We use a dual-element probe, calibrate on a step block of the same material, and watch the A-scan display so we can tell a true back wall from a doubled echo. Where the surface is too rough to read, we note it in the report and recommend local surface preparation instead of recording a doubtful number.

faq.q: Does ultrasonic testing replace radiography for weld examination?
faq.a: Only where the construction code and the owner allow it. Some codes, such as parts of ASME B31.3 and AWS D1.1, contain ultrasonic acceptance rules for production welds. The choice is agreed with the owner, the engineer and the authorized inspector before the job, so it is a scope decision, not something a technician decides on the day.

faq.q: Who decides if a thin reading is acceptable?
faq.a: The owner's inspector or engineer does. We supply measured thickness and indication data against the nominal and minimum values you give us. For API 510, 570 and 653 equipment, the owner's authorized inspector remains responsible for the inspection and applies the corrosion-rate and remaining-life calculation.

faq.q: Can you inspect stainless steel brewing and process tanks in West Michigan?
faq.a: Yes, thickness gauging works on austenitic stainless steel with the right probe and couplant, and we take care not to contaminate product-contact surfaces. Cast or coarse-grained stainless can scatter sound, so we confirm the material and the surface before quoting.

faq.q: How cold is too cold for ultrasonic work in a Grand Rapids winter?
faq.a: There is no single number, because couplant, probe and instrument each have limits. In sub-freezing weather we use low-temperature couplant, remove frost and snow from the scan surface and often add a windbreak or heater. If conditions make a reliable reading unlikely, we say so and propose a safer time window.

faq.q: What do I need to send to get a UT quote?
faq.a: Send the equipment list or drawings, the governing code or specification, the materials and nominal thickness, the surface condition, the operating temperature, any insulation to be removed and the preferred dates. A short site description with access notes helps us choose the right equipment and crew size.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Grand Rapids?
faq.a: No. Technicians are mobilized from our teams to your site for the agreed scope. This lets us match qualified personnel to the code and the equipment, and it means travel and access are planned with you at the quote stage rather than assumed.

Our written practice follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II technicians perform and interpret the examination, and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. If your contract demands a different qualification scheme, tell us when you ask for a quote so we can confirm whether we can meet it.
